articles.headline: Shooting stars from a famous comet
articles.standfirst: This week, tiny pieces of Halley's Comet will make lines of light in the night sky.
body: Look up this week! The Orionid meteor shower comes every October, and this year it is at its best on the night of 21 to 22 October.

People often call meteors 'shooting stars', but they are not stars. They are very small pieces of dust from Halley's Comet, a famous comet. When the Earth travels through this dust, the pieces fall into the air around our planet very fast – about 66 kilometres every second. They get very hot and make short lines of light in the sky.

On a dark night, you can see between 10 and 20 meteors in one hour. But this year the Moon is big and bright, so it is harder to see some of them. The best time is early in the morning, after the Moon goes down and before the sun comes up.
You don't need a telescope. Find a safe place with a big view of the sky, and just watch!

articles.headline: The Lord of Miracles visits the Government Palace
articles.standfirst: For the first time in 40 years, Peru's most famous religious image came into the palace in Lima.
body: The Lord of Miracles is a famous painting of Jesus Christ in Lima. People also call it the 'Brown Christ'. Every October, many Peruvians walk with the image through the streets of the city. It is one of the most important religious traditions in Peru.
On Sunday, the image visited the Government Palace in Lima. It was a special day, because it was the first time in 40 years. The last visit was in 1986.
The President of Peru and the ministers were there to welcome it. In the courtyard of the palace, there was a big carpet made of flowers, with pictures about Peru.

Members of the Lord of Miracles brotherhood carried the image on their shoulders. Soldiers from the president's guard were there too. For many Peruvians, the Lord of Miracles is a symbol of faith and hope.

articles.headline: Up, over and down again: a car that flies like a rocket
articles.standfirst: Elon Musk says Tesla's new sports car is the world's first flying car – but you can't fly it on the road.
body: Elon Musk, the billionaire who runs the car company Tesla and the space company SpaceX, has shown a new sports car which, he says, is the world's first flying car. The Tesla Roadster 2 was presented last Thursday at a SpaceX centre in Texas, where the company develops and tests its rockets.

The car uses technology from SpaceX. It has small rocket engines called thrusters, which push it into the air. In a video of the event, the car drives up a curved ramp, holds on upside down and then uses its thrusters to flip over, fly and land again. Later, it jumps over a line of other Tesla cars. Nobody was driving it from the inside: the car was controlled from a distance.
Musk also said that the Roadster 2 could go from 0 to 60 miles per hour (about 97 kilometres per hour) in less than one second, which would be a record. 'Flying cars are real,' he said.

Not everyone will be able to fly one, though. Musk said he was not sure that the car was legal everywhere, and the company says that flying it is not allowed on public roads. A one-seat 'rocket' version with a full flight system will only be available by invitation.

The car will not be cheap. It is expected to cost more than $200,000, and production should start in 2028. Back in 2014 Musk did not believe in flying cars. He announced the Roadster 2 three years later, in 2017.

articles.headline: More houses, more trade: Peru's economy keeps growing
articles.standfirst: Official figures show that most parts of the Peruvian economy grew in August – but fishing had a bad month.
body: Good news for Peru: the country's economy is growing. In August 2026, Peru produced 3.23% more goods and services than in August 2025. The figures were published last Thursday by the National Institute of Statistics and Informatics (INEI), the government office that collects official numbers about the country.

When economists say that an economy 'grows', they mean that people and companies are producing and selling more – for example, more houses, more food and more services. INEI said that most sectors of the economy grew in August.

The star of the month was construction, which rose by 10.34%. Trade, which includes buying and selling things in shops and markets, went up by 6.89%, and electricity, gas and water grew by 6.61%. Factories produced 4.18% more, while agriculture and livestock farming increased by 3.37%. Hotels and restaurants also grew, but only a little: 1.20%.

However, not every sector had a good month. Fishing fell by 17.33%, and mining and hydrocarbons, such as oil and gas, dropped by 5.53%. These two sectors went down while almost all the others went up.

Over a longer period, the picture is also positive. Between January and August 2026, the economy grew by 3.14% compared with the same months of 2025. And over the last twelve months, from September 2025 to August 2026, it grew by 3.31%.

articles.headline: Out of a clear blue sky: the invisible bumps that worry pilots
articles.standfirst: A warming planet is making one of the hardest kinds of turbulence to predict more common. Here is what scientists and airlines are doing about it.
articles.instructions: For each question, choose the paragraph (A–E). Paragraphs may be chosen more than once.
body: A. Most people think of turbulence as something caused by storms. Thunderstorms are full of rising and falling air, but pilots can usually see them on radar and fly around them. There is, however, another kind of turbulence that is much harder to avoid. Clear-air turbulence appears at cruising height, often at the edges of jet streams – the fast rivers of air that flow around the Earth – and no radar can detect it in advance.

B. Scientists believe the problem is getting worse. A University of Reading study of atmospheric data from 1979 to 2020 found that severe clear-air turbulence had increased by 55%, while moderate and light turbulence had risen by 37% and 17%. Even if global warming is limited to 1.5C, a further 27% rise is expected; with 2.75C of warming, the figure could reach 56%.

C. According to Todd Lane, a professor at the University of Melbourne, for every degree of warming the atmosphere can hold 7% more water vapour, which is the fuel of thunderstorms. Rising temperatures can also change the difference in temperature between the equator and the poles, increasing wind shear – sudden changes in wind speed or direction – in the jet streams.

D. The risks are real. Turbulence is the leading cause of injuries to passengers and crew in non-fatal accidents, says the International Air Transport Association (IATA). In 2024, a flight from London to Singapore hit severe turbulence over Myanmar and 79 people were seriously hurt. The ten most turbulent routes in the world all cross either the Andes or the Himalayas.

E. The industry is fighting back. Since 2018, IATA has collected turbulence data from sensors on more than 3,700 aircraft belonging to about 30 airlines, and AI tools now turn it into almost instant warnings. Some manufacturers are testing Lidar, which uses lasers to study the air ahead of a plane. Anyone can also check a forecast on Turbli, a website built by engineer Ignacio Gallego-Marcos.

articles.headline: A capital in the jungle, waiting for its people
articles.standfirst: Indonesia has built a brand-new capital city in the rainforest of Borneo. So why does it feel so empty?
body: Deep in the rainforest of Borneo, Indonesia has built something extraordinary: a brand-new capital city. Nusantara, in the province of East Kalimantan, has a presidential palace, modern offices, tall apartment blocks and wide roads. What it does not have, at least for now, is many people. Planners hoped it would hold 1.2 million residents by 2029, yet only around 10,000 have moved there so far.

To understand why the city was built, you have to look at Jakarta, more than 1,200 kilometres away. Last year the current capital, home to almost 42 million people, overtook Tokyo to become the world's most populous city. It suffers from heavy traffic and poor air, but its biggest problem is that it is sinking: about 40% of Jakarta lies below sea level, and parts of the north still flood regularly in the rainy season.

The idea of moving the capital is decades old, but it was former president Joko Widodo who decided in 2019 to build a new one in the jungle. Construction began in 2022, with the long-term aim of housing 1.9 million people by 2045, the 100th anniversary of Indonesia's independence.

Since then, however, priorities have changed. Under the current president, Prabowo Subianto, the city's yearly budget has been cut sharply, from 43 trillion rupiah in 2024 to 6.3 trillion in 2026, while money has moved to other projects, such as a national school meals programme. A regulation aims to make Nusantara the 'political capital' by 2028, but this year Indonesia's Constitutional Court ruled that Jakarta will remain the official capital until a further decree is signed.

Meanwhile, the few people who live in the new towers – about 1,800 public servants and security staff – are getting used to the calm. One young government worker admitted that the city is quiet, but said that this is better for her mental health, and that residents fill their free time with book clubs, journals and conversation.

articles.headline: Ten years' notice: the blood signals that could reveal a gut disease early
articles.standfirst: Antibody patterns appear long before inflammatory bowel disease is diagnosed, a new study suggests – raising hopes of earlier treatment and, one day, prevention.
body: For most patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), treatment begins only after the symptoms do – and by then, the gut has often already been damaged. A new study suggests that this need not always be the case: the immune system appears to send out warning signals as much as a decade before the condition is diagnosed.

IBD, which affects at least 3.8 million people worldwide, causes long-term inflammation of the digestive tract, leading to pain and fatigue. Its two main forms are Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Its exact cause remains unknown, although genetics, the microbes that live in the gut and a misfiring immune system are all thought to play a part. Many patients do not respond to existing drugs, and a significant number eventually need surgery.

The research team, led by Dr Arno Bourgonje of the University Medical Centre Groningen in the Netherlands and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York, and working with colleagues in Vienna, analysed 2,000 blood samples taken from 500 members of the US military. Of these people, 200 later developed Crohn's disease, 200 developed ulcerative colitis and 100 developed neither. The samples were screened for antibodies against hundreds of thousands of protein fragments from bacteria, viruses, food and the body's own tissues.

Distinct patterns emerged. People who went on to develop Crohn's disease more often carried antibodies against the Epstein-Barr virus, which causes glandular fever, and the difference was already visible ten years before diagnosis. The signal was strongest in those who later developed the most severe, complicated form. In ulcerative colitis, by contrast, the pattern included antibodies against one of the body's own proteins.

The researchers are careful not to overstate their results. Bourgonje stressed that this is "not yet a test" that can tell someone they will become ill. The findings show a link rather than proof that infections cause IBD, and they need to be confirmed in other groups of people. An independent expert, Professor James Lindsay of Barts Health, called the techniques a research tool that is not ready for use in clinics.

Even so, the hope is that IBD may one day follow the path of type 1 diabetes, where a blood test can identify people whose immune system has started to attack the body before any symptoms appear, allowing treatment that delays the disease. The study was published in the journal Gut.

articles.headline: A market leaning on a few giants: how the AI boom tilted Wall Street
articles.standfirst: A handful of artificial intelligence companies now account for a remarkable share of the US stock market's growth. Experts say that concentration brings risks of its own.
body: Few industries have grown as quickly as artificial intelligence. Shares in the companies that design AI chips, build data centres and develop AI tools have soared; one Australian investment manager, Steve Johnson, called some of them among the fastest-growing businesses ever seen. Yet an analysis by the Australian broadcaster suggests that the boom is making the US stock market lopsided.

Take the S&P 500, the index of the 500 largest companies listed in the United States. Technology firms now account for about 44% of its total value, and the chip maker Nvidia has become the most valuable company in the world. Since April, roughly 230 of the 500 companies have seen their share prices fall. Yet their losses were more than cancelled out by the gains of just three giants: Meta, Microsoft and Apple.

Add three chip makers – Nvidia, Micron and AMD – and these six companies explain 57% of the index's total gains since April. Without them, the S&P 500 would have risen by only 4.35% in six months, less than half its actual growth of 10%. According to Angel Zhong, an economist at RMIT University, the top ten stocks made up about 27% of the index at the height of the dot-com bubble in 2000; recently, the figure has been about 39%.

Unlike in 2000, when enormous valuations were driven largely by hype, some of today's AI firms, notably the chip makers, are already highly profitable. But Zhong points out that the leading AI labs earn only a fraction of what is being spent on their behalf, and that a boom originally paid for out of profits increasingly depends on outside money, including a great deal of debt.

A further concern is what has been called circular financing. Nvidia invests so heavily in its own biggest customers that it has been compared to a bank. For example, it agreed to invest in OpenAI's infrastructure; OpenAI then signed a huge contract to use Oracle's data centres; and Oracle, in turn, buys Nvidia chips to fill them. The firms, Zhong says, are "each other's investors, suppliers and customers", which makes it harder to judge how much demand for AI is genuine.
None of this means that a crash is inevitable. But it ties these companies' fortunes together, and when so much of a market's growth rests on so few shoulders, a stumble by one could be felt by all.
